subtype: Approach: rechecks the backward chain against real progress and reschedules [Revision]
passage: At month three of the plan, Salma's checkpoint, finishing the first reading block, had slipped by two weeks, because quarter-end at the firm swallowed her evenings. The finance qualification exam sat in November. Salma, a young analyst, pushed her chair back on a noisy Saturday, with a wedding band playing next door, and pulled the sheet toward her. Instead of squeezing the old dates, she started from the exam again: last mock in mid-October, so practice must end by then, so the second reading block must finish by late August. Then she looked at the optional data certificate she had added in a keen moment. It no longer fit. She struck it out and sent Mahima, her study partner, the new dates that night.

qa.q: Why had Salma's month-three checkpoint slipped?
qa.a: It had slipped because quarter-end at the firm swallowed her evenings.

qa.q: What was Salma probably feeling as she looked at the slipped checkpoint?
qa.a: Salma was probably worried and pressed for time, but she chose to redo the dates from the exam instead of panicking.

qa.q: What other approach could help Salma keep the new dates?
qa.a: Salma could ask her manager for a few study days close to the exam, since a fixed block of free time protects the last stretch of the plan.

qa.q: How might Mahima see the new dates?
qa.a: Mahima would probably feel glad to have clear dates and see that Salma is facing the slip honestly, though maybe a little worried about the tighter schedule.

grounding: Shows an analyst noticing a slipping checkpoint, re-deriving later milestones from the exam date and dropping an optional certificate.

subtype: Approach: combines backward planning with buffers and a checklist [Action]
passage: I'm Keerthana, and I sit across from Tushar, who was building a small app to launch before Diwali. On Monday Tushar wrote 'Launch: 20 October' on the whiteboard, then wrote backwards: store review, testing, payment integration, login. Then Tushar drew a line two weeks ahead of the launch date, wrote 'slack' in it, and said, 'Reviews always take longer than they say.' Every dependent task went onto a shared checklist that we could all tick. I watched that list for six weeks. When the payment provider ran ten days late, the slack absorbed it and the launch date did not move. I can't tell whether Tushar was anxious the whole time, but the list was the first thing Tushar opened every morning.

qa.q: What launch date did Tushar write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Tushar wrote 'Launch: 20 October'.

qa.q: What might Tushar have been feeling while opening the checklist every morning?
qa.a: Tushar may have been careful and a little anxious, though Keerthana cannot be sure of the inner state.

qa.q: What other step could Tushar add to protect the date?
qa.a: Tushar could give each risky task an owner and a small demo date, since early demos show a delay before it eats into the slack.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt watching the slack absorb the delay?
qa.a: Keerthana was probably impressed and reassured, since the launch date did not move.

grounding: Shows an engineer working back from a festival-season release date, adding two weeks of slack and tracking dependent tasks on a shared checklist.

subtype: Approach: imagines the plan has already failed and lists reasons [Thinking]
passage: On Wednesday the fest committee chalked out the stalls in the school hall. Minakshi, who was running the lemonade and snacks stall, sat on the steps with Vasudha and a notebook. 'Imagine it's Saturday night and the stall flopped,' she said. 'Why?' She wrote as they talked: not enough change ready, so people walk off; rain, and the stall is in the open courtyard; a poor spot behind the science block. Vasudha added, 'And the sugar might run out by noon.' Minakshi hadn't thought of any of that when she had only planned how many people would come. Beside each item she wrote a small fix: coins from the shop counter at home, a tarp from the caretaker, asking the committee to swap the spot, and double the sugar.

qa.q: Which reasons for a flop did Minakshi write herself?
qa.a: Minakshi wrote not enough change ready, rain in the open courtyard, and a poor spot behind the science block.

qa.q: What does the notebook suggest about how Minakshi now feels about the stall?
qa.a: Minakshi seems more prepared and realistic, having seen that her first plan was too hopeful.

qa.q: What other approach could Minakshi use to find more risks?
qa.a: Minakshi could ask a teacher or senior who ran a stall last year what went wrong for them, since they may know problems she has not met.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have seen the exercise?
qa.a: Vasudha probably felt useful, since adding the sugar risk showed that two people spot more than one.

grounding: Shows a teenager imagining that the fest stall flopped and writing down reasons in advance, which surfaces risks that hopeful planning skipped.

subtype: Approach: turns each imagined failure into a preventive step [Action]
passage:
Hi Sonali,

Before Saturday, can we try something? Imagine it's Sunday evening and we lost. Why? I wrote down two big reasons. One: the venue's internet is patchy, and our model needs a download. Two: I'm the only one who has written any code so far, so if I get stuck or fall ill, we're finished. Here's what I've done about them. I booked a phone data plan for the weekend and already saved the model files on the laptop. And I split the app into three parts: mine is the model, yours is the front end, and Ravi has the data cleaning. Can you look at the split and tell me if the front end is too much?

Tejas

qa.q: Who has the data cleaning?
qa.a: Ravi has the data cleaning.

qa.q: What is Tejas worried about?
qa.a: Tejas is worried about being the only coder, since getting stuck or ill would leave the team unable to finish.

qa.q: What other step could the team add to lower the risk further?
qa.a: The team could hold a short check-in each evening to see who is stuck, since a problem found early is easier to share out.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel about the front-end part?
qa.a: Sonali may feel a little pressed by the workload but relieved that the coding is now shared.

grounding: Shows a student team imagining losing a hackathon, listing weak internet and one person doing all the coding, then booking a data plan and splitting the work among three.

subtype: Approach: imagines so many failures that starting feels impossible [Pitfall]
passage:
'Fifty-one,' said Dhruv, tapping the notebook. 'That's how many ways the food-truck idea can collapse.'
'Fifty-one?' said Vidya, flipping pages. 'Fuel, permits, rain, a rival, a bad cook, a stolen generator...'
'Right. And each one is possible. I feel sick reading it.'
'Which is the most likely?'
'I don't know. They all look equally bad.'
'So how do you decide what to worry about first?'
Dhruv closed the notebook. 'I don't. Maybe I shouldn't start.'
'You haven't even tried one weekend.'
'Fifty-one reasons, Vidya.'
Vidya sighed. 'Reasons, sure. But you haven't marked which are likely or which would hurt most. It's just a heap.'

qa.q: How many ways to collapse did Dhruv list?
qa.a: Dhruv listed fifty-one ways.

qa.q: How does Dhruv feel when reading the list?
qa.a: Dhruv feels sick and full of dread, and is leaning toward not starting at all.

qa.q: What other approach could Dhruv try with the list?
qa.a: Dhruv could mark each risk for how likely it is and how much damage it does, keep the top few, and run one small weekend test.

qa.q: How does Vidya see the list?
qa.a: Vidya sees it as a heap without ranking and not a reason to quit, and the sigh suggests some frustration.

grounding: Shows a student listing dozens of ways a startup could fail and feeling dread, without ranking the risks, so the exercise becomes a reason not to begin.

subtype: Approach: runs a short team pre-mortem before a client demo [Thinking]
passage: The afternoon before the client demo in a Lisbon office, Ines handed out sticky notes and said, 'Write privately: it's tomorrow at ten, and the demo has failed. Why?' Six people wrote in silence for three minutes and folded their notes. Ines read them aloud without names. The confident planners had listed the projector, running late and too many slides. Freya, who rarely spoke in meetings, had written that the sample data took four minutes to load, and someone else added that the login page failed on the client's network. Nobody had mentioned either. Ines wrote both at the top of the board. By evening Freya had saved the sample data locally, and another colleague tested the login on a guest network.

qa.q: How many minutes did the team write in silence?
qa.a: They wrote in silence for three minutes.

qa.q: What might Freya have felt about speaking up in meetings, and how did the notes help?
qa.a: Freya probably felt hesitant, since Freya rarely spoke in meetings, and writing privately took away that pressure.

qa.q: What other step could the team take about the login risk?
qa.a: The team could ask the client beforehand which network and login they will use, since it answers the question before the demo.

qa.q: How might the confident planners have felt when the notes were read out?
qa.a: They were probably surprised and a little humbled, since nobody had mentioned the data or login risks.

grounding: Shows a team lead asking each colleague to write privately why the demo would fail, and quiet members raising data-loading and login risks the confident planners missed.

subtype: Approach: ranks imagined failures and revises the plan around the top three [Revision]
passage: Indu, come, let me tell you about the launch that taught me to sort my worries. I'm Minakshi, and I was a new manager then. We ran a pre-mortem, and the board filled with thirty-odd ideas: printers, pigeons on the roof, a vendor's mood. Next morning I looked at it and my stomach dropped; it was a wall of worry and I couldn't act on any of it. So I sat with a pen and marked each idea twice: how likely, and how costly. Only three scored high on both: the payment gateway going down, our one trained person falling ill, and stock arriving late. For those I planned backups. The rest I decided to live with. A pigeon did cause a hiccup, and we laughed. The gateway did stumble, and the backup carried us.

qa.q: Which three risks did Minakshi keep?
qa.a: Minakshi kept the payment gateway going down, the one trained person falling ill, and stock arriving late.

qa.q: What did Minakshi feel on looking at the board the next morning?
qa.a: Minakshi felt overwhelmed, as Minakshi's stomach dropped at a wall of worry that could not be acted on.

qa.q: Which choice turned the list from a wall of worry into a plan, and why?
qa.a: Marking each idea for how likely and how costly it was, and keeping only those high on both, gave backups for the few risks that mattered.

qa.q: How might the team have felt when the gateway stumbled and the backup carried them?
qa.a: They were probably relieved and reassured that the plan had worked, after having already laughed at the pigeon hiccup.

grounding: Shows a manager noticing an unfocused pre-mortem list, keeping the three risks that are both likely and costly, planning for those and accepting the rest.

subtype: Approach: picks a tool that closes the gap in front of them [Action]
passage: Camila, five, stood in the kitchen and looked up at the biscuit tin on the top shelf. She jumped. Too far. She looked at the gap between her hand and the tin, then at the small wooden stool by the door. She dragged it, scrape, scrape, across the floor and pushed it under the shelf. Her uncle Yuki came in and held the stool with both hands. Camila climbed up carefully and grabbed the tin. It was heavy, and she wobbled. 'Give it to me,' said Uncle Yuki, and lifted it down. They each took one biscuit.

qa.q: What did Camila drag across the floor?
qa.a: Camila dragged the small wooden stool across the floor.

qa.q: What does Camila want?
qa.a: Camila wants the biscuit tin on the top shelf, and she is determined to reach it, so she fetches the stool.

qa.q: What could Camila do if the stool was still too low?
qa.a: Camila could ask Uncle Yuki to reach the tin for her instead of climbing higher.

qa.q: How might Uncle Yuki have felt watching Camila climb?
qa.a: Uncle Yuki was probably a little worried, which is why he held the stool and then lifted the heavy tin down.

grounding: Shows a child who wants a tin on a high shelf noticing the gap in height and dragging over a stool as the means to shrink it.

subtype: Approach: compares where things are with where they should be and picks a step that shrinks the gap [Thinking]
passage: Vikas wanted his cycle at school in the morning, but the back tyre was flat. 'What's missing?' he thought. 'Air. So I need a pump.' He found the hand pump under the stairs and fitted it on, but the air hissed out at the join. The pump's nozzle didn't fit the tyre's little valve. 'New gap. The fit.' He remembered that his father had a small brass piece for that. He ran to the yard where his father was tying up the buffalo. 'Papa, do you have the adapter?' His father took it from his pocket and gave it to him. His sister Sangeeta held the cycle steady while he pumped. The tyre grew round, and Vikas rang the bell twice.

qa.q: Where did Vikas find the hand pump?
qa.a: Vikas found the hand pump under the stairs.

qa.q: What was Vikas thinking when the air hissed out at the join?
qa.a: Vikas saw a new problem, the fit between the nozzle and the valve, and was probably a little frustrated but still determined.

qa.q: What could Vikas do if his father did not have the adapter?
qa.a: Vikas could ask a neighbour or the cycle repair shop nearby, since they may have the piece that closes the gap.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt while holding the cycle steady?
qa.a: Sangeeta was probably proud and curious, watching her brother solve the problem step by step.

grounding: Shows a boy comparing where the cycle is with where it should be, finding the pump first, then noticing the valve fit and asking his father for the adapter.

subtype: Approach: breaks a large gap into subgoals when the direct step is blocked [Thinking]
passage: I'm Mohit, and at sixteen I had to get myself across the city to a coaching class with nobody to drop me. The whole trip felt too big to solve, so I stopped trying to solve it. I asked only: how do I reach the bus stop? That was easy, ten minutes on foot. Next question: which bus? A neighbour's sister told me the number 47 goes past the centre. Third: the fare. I checked with the conductor and put two coins aside every day for a week. Each piece was small enough to fix alone, and stacked together they made a route. I gave my mother the route and my arrival time. On Monday I took the 47, arrived ten minutes early, and felt taller than I had in weeks.

qa.q: Which bus goes past the coaching centre?
qa.a: The number 47 goes past the centre.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel on arriving early?
qa.a: Mohit felt taller, meaning proud and more confident, after solving the trip piece by piece.

qa.q: What other approach could Mohit use to make the journey easier?
qa.a: Mohit could ask a classmate from the centre to travel together on some days, since company makes a long journey safer and simpler.

qa.q: How might Mohit's mother see the plan?
qa.a: Mohit's mother was probably reassured by having the route and arrival time, and glad Mohit had thought it through.

grounding: Shows a student who cannot get a lift to a coaching centre and breaks the trip into subgoals: reaching the bus stop, finding the bus number and arranging the fare.
